items.name: The blood-to-the-stomach story
body: Digestion does increase blood flow
to the gut. The rest does not follow.
The Sleep Foundation concludes that
scientific evidence has debunked the
myth, because cerebral autoregulation
keeps brain blood flow stable.

items.name: The dip runs on a schedule
body: In a 2005 review in Clinics in Sports
Medicine, sleep researcher Timothy
Monk described the post-lunch dip as
having its roots in human biology.
He tied it to a roughly 12-hour part
of the circadian system.

items.name: Sleep debt does the rest
body: The dip shows up in some people even
without a meal, and is exacerbated by
a high-carbohydrate lunch.
CDC's National Center for Health
Statistics reported that in 2024, 30.5%
of US adults slept under seven hours.

items.name: Meal size is the clearest lever
body: In a 2012 crossover study in Physiology
and Behavior, Reyner and colleagues
restricted 12 young men to five hours
of sleep.
A 922-calorie lunch beat a 305-calorie
one for lane drifting and sleepy EEG,
with the gap opening after 30 minutes.

items.name: Protein blunts the route
body: Research from Richard Wurtman's lab
found that as little as 5% of a meal's
calories from protein is enough to
block the shift that lets extra
tryptophan into the brain.
Eggs, yogurt, fish or beans will do.

items.name: Walk for a few minutes
body: A 2022 review and meta-analysis of
seven studies in Sports Medicine
found that breaking up sitting with
two to five minutes of light walking
every 20 to 30 minutes lowered
post-meal glucose and insulin.

items.name: Daylight, and a short nap
body: Bright light is the strongest input to
the circadian clock that is producing
the dip in the first place.
If the dip lands at a predictable hour,
keeping a nap brief avoids waking
out of deep sleep groggy.

headline: The circadian dip would have
arrived with or without lunch.
A heavy meal deepens it, most
of all when you are short on sleep.
tip: and walk a few minutes afterward.
